extracted.intended_audience: federal agency officials and staff responsible for notice-and-comment rulemaking, eRulemaking program/OIRA/coordinating bodies
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for agencies on identifying, processing, and publicly managing mass, computer-generated, and malattributed comments in notice-and-comment rulemaking dockets to preserve informational value, transparency, and legitimacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory and procedural obligation to process and consider comments
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the Administrative Procedure Act (APA), agencies must give members of the public notice of proposed rules and the opportunity to comment; agencies create and maintain an online public rulemaking docket to collect and publish comments, and must process, read, analyze, and seriously consider any significant comment from a person or organization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This requirement frames agencies' responsibilities: the process is designed to improve rule quality by receiving information and public scrutiny. Citations include 5 U.S.C. § 553 and case law (e.g., Am. Mining Cong. v. EPA; Home Box Office, Inc. v. FCC).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: mass comment campaign
rubrics_metrics.description: A mass comment campaign is characterized by members of the public orchestrating the submission of a large number of identical or nearly identical comments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Challenges include agencies having to process large numbers of only slightly different comments and difficulty digesting/analyzing overall content; mass campaigns may also affect perceptions of rulemaking legitimacy and strain agency resources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: computer-generated comments
rubrics_metrics.description: Computer-generated comments are comments that are generated by software algorithms rather than humans.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legal considerations arise because the APA affords an opportunity to comment to 'interested persons'; distinguishing algorithmic from human comments can be difficult. Because they are not produced by a human, informational value may be limited or compromised and agencies may be misled.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: malattributed comments
rubrics_metrics.description: Malattributed comments are comments falsely attributed to persons who did not, in fact, submit them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Malattribution is enabled by online datasets of personal information and simple automation tools; malattributed comments may mislead agencies, harm individuals whose identities are used, and raise potential criminal or administrative issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tailor recommendations to agency programs and comment types
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies should tailor the suggestions in this Recommendation to their particular rulemaking programs and the types of comments they receive or expect to receive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Not all agencies will encounter these problems; resource constraints and the nature of an agency’s docket may justify adopting some or none of the recommendations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publish policy statements about posting and use of mass/computer-generated/malattributed comments
rubrics_metrics.description: When needed, agencies should publish policy statements about the posting and use of mass, computer-generated, and malattributed comments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These statements should take into account the meaningfulness of public participation and balance user-friendliness, transparency, and informational completeness. Agencies may provide for exceptions in appropriate circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Policy options for handling identical or nearly identical comments
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies should consider including different approaches in their policies with respect to identical or nearly identical comments, including the option to: (a) post a single representative example with a count and an option to view all comments; (b) break out and post non-identical content; or (c) ask organizers to submit a single comment with multiple signatures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies may use eRulemaking site capabilities or other technologies to implement these options; choice should reflect tradeoffs among accessibility, analytical usefulness, and transparency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Policy against malattributed comments and remediation approach
rubrics_metrics.description: An agency policy against submission of malattributed comments should provide that if the agency is aware it has received such a comment, it either will retain the comment but remove the malattribution (render it anonymous) or remove the comment from the docket altogether.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: At minimum, if a malattributed comment remains, the agency must anonymize it to protect the person whose identity was used.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide explanatory materials to prospective commenters
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies and coordinating bodies should consider providing materials that explain to prospective commenters what information is useful to an agency in a public comment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These materials could take various formats (videos, FAQs) and may appear in an agency's notice of proposed rulemaking or website; they should explain the purpose of the comment process and that agencies seriously consider substantive public comments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ask specific questions and identify useful information in notices
rubrics_metrics.description: In notices of proposed rulemaking, notices of inquiry, and advance notices of proposed rulemaking, agencies should ask specific questions and identify particular types of information that would be useful in developing the proposal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Framing requests for input with specific questions increases the likelihood of receiving focused, informative comments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Access to software that identifies unique content and extracts meaning
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies should have access to reliable and appropriate software to identify the unique content in submitted comments and to extract meaningful information from comments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such software should provide enhanced search options based on unique content to assist agencies in digesting and analyzing comment dockets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use human-verification technologies for comment submission
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies that operate commenting platforms should consider using technology that verifies that a commenter is a human being, such as reCAPTCHA or similar identity-proofing tools.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This verification is distinct from identity validation technologies that force commenters to prove their identity; it helps guard against automated submissions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide a common de-duplication platform
rubrics_metrics.description: The eRulemaking Program should provide a common de-duplication platform for agencies to use, although agencies should be free to modify it or use another platform as appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: De-duplication tools can help identify and group duplicate or near-duplicate comments so agencies can manage mass submissions more effectively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coordinate with relevant bodies and share best practices
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies should work closely with relevant coordinating bodies (e.g., eRulemaking Program, OIRA, working groups) to improve technologies and develop new approaches addressing mass, computer-generated, and malattributed comments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies and coordinating bodies should share best practices and innovations for addressing these challenges across government.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ongoing training and staff development
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies should offer opportunities for ongoing training and staff development to respond to the rapidly evolving technologies related to mass, computer-generated, and malattributed comments and public participation more generally.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Training helps staff identify, analyze, and appropriately manage problematic comments and new participation platforms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advance articulation or disclosure when excluding/removing comments
rubrics_metrics.description: If an agency decides to exclude or remove any mass, computer-generated, and malattributed comments from the docket, it should articulate such a policy in advance or disclose in the docket why it is excluding the comment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Transparency about exclusion/removal policies preserves public trust and helps the public understand docket contents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not discard computer-generated comments unless devoid of informational value
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies should not discard the computer-generated comments they receive unless those comments contain no informational value; when storing these comments, agencies may segregate or treat them separately.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Segregation and separate treatment allow agencies to preserve records and analyze whether algorithmic comments contain useful information without conflating them with human submissions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Retain and place in docket any comment the agency relies on
rubrics_metrics.description: Any comment on which an agency actually relies should be placed and retained in the rulemaking docket, including malattributed and computer-generated comments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When placing such comments in the docket, agencies should anonymize malattributed comments and consider segregating or flagging computer-generated comments to preserve transparency and protect individuals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide mechanisms to request removal of malattributed comments
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies should provide opportunities (including potentially after the comment deadline) for individuals whose names have been attached to comments they did not submit to identify and request removal of such malattributed comments from the docket.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Responsive channels for individuals to report misuse of their identity help protect privacy and docket integrity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Notify submitters when comments are flagged, removed, or anonymized
rubrics_metrics.description: If an agency flags a comment as malattributed or computer-generated, or removes such a comment from the docket, and the submitter provided electronic contact information, the agency should notify the submitter of the agency’s action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notifying submitters improves transparency and allows legitimate commenters to correct or follow up as necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclose in final rule whether malattributed or computer-generated comments were removed
rubrics_metrics.description: When publishing a final rule, agencies should state whether they removed from the docket any malattributed or computer-generated comments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This practice promotes transparency about how agency decisions were informed and any exclusions that occurred during the comment period.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monitor and evaluate new technologies to facilitate informative participation
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies and coordinating bodies should stay abreast of new technologies, platforms, and processes for facilitating informative public participation in rulemaking, particularly where such developments might reduce burdens in discerning useful information from problematic comments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because technologies are evolving, agencies should consider whether emerging tools might improve management of mass, computer-generated, and malattributed comments and promote meaningful participation.
